science.title: Machine learning based distribution mapping of gold in soil samples using aqua regia digestion and solid phase extraction
science.description: In the present work, aqua regia followed by solid phase extraction using activated carbon was developed for soil sample treatment. The analytical approach was further integrated with machine learning algorithms enabling the prediction of gold potential zone. Some modifications such as roasting the samples and hydrofluoric acid addition for silicon structure removal of the samples have also been investigated. The analytical performance of the method was evaluated via certified reference materials and geological samples, at different concentration levels. Random Forest, Gaussian Process Regression and Ordinary Kriging models were subsequently used considering nonlinear spatial relationships, uncertainty prediction and generate predictive gold distribution map. Despite the significant effect of sample roasting, HF addition had only a minor and negligible effect (according to t-test at 95% confidence level) and the proposed method was able to detect gold concentrations ranging from 18.0 ng/g to 53,000 ng/g in soil samples and down to 0.01 µg/mL in aqueous samples with correlation coefficients greater than 0.9991. The method accuracy and precision were in the range of 3.7–9.6 and − 9.5-+7.4, respectively. Comparison of responses obtained for the analysis of 40 different geological samples via fire assay and aqua regia digestion shows a good compatibility which verified the aqua regia as a simple, low cost and reliable treatment technique.

science.title: In the synthetic biology era, engineered fungi could mitigate carbon dioxide emissions and enhance environmental resilience
science.description: Over the past two decades, there has been a staggering increase in greenhouse gas emissions, particularly carbon dioxide (CO2) from unrestrained anthropogenic activities, leading to notable environmental shifts. Despite continuous efforts to reduce emissions, the world is not making satisfactory progress, which calls for immediate action to implement alternative strategies to enhance environmental sustainability. The Earth naturally absorbs and stores carbon through various processes, but merely keeping pace with ongoing human activities is no longer sufficient. Land plants and marine prokaryotes absorb CO2 during photosynthesis and store carbon as biomass. Eukaryotic organisms also represent a valuable resource that can provide insights into the biological fixation and removal of atmospheric CO2. Expanding the capacities of Earth’s natural systems offers enormous potential for enhancing carbon sinks and promoting environmental resilience. Although extensive synthetic engineering of plant systems has been conducted to enhance their native carbon fixation pathways, research on microorganisms, especially fungi, has been limited. In this review, we specifically explore the role of soil-borne fungi in carbon management, elucidating their responses to environmental shifts and their potential for climate change mitigation. We place particular emphasis on the role of various fungal guilds in this process, highlighting those that should be prioritized for future synthetic biology applications. We then engage with previous endeavors to address primary challenges in advancing genetic tools for these understudied fungi. Lastly, we discuss how integrating synthetic biology practices into the field of soil-associated fungi can drive advances in long-term carbon storage, enhance degradation of environmental pollutants, and improve nutrient exchange and soil health, contributing to more resilient soil ecosystems and sustainable environmental interventions. Rising carbon dioxide emissions from human activities are driving environmental change and increasing the need for strategies that strengthen natural carbon sinks and ecosystem resilience. While plants and microorganisms play important roles in carbon capture and storage, the potential of soil-associated fungi remains comparatively underexplored, particularly from a synthetic biology perspective. In this Review, we examine the roles of soil-borne fungi in carbon management, their responses to environmental change, and their potential contributions to climate change mitigation. We highlight key fungal guilds that could be prioritized for future synthetic biology applications and discuss current challenges in developing genetic tools for understudied fungi. Finally, we explore how engineering soil-associated fungi could support long-term carbon storage while providing broader environmental benefits, including pollutant degradation, nutrient exchange, and improved soil health. Together, these opportunities position fungal synthetic biology as a promising approach for developing more resilient soil ecosystems and sustainable environmental interventions. Soil fungi are an underexplored tool for climate mitigation, as discussed in this synthesis, which examines how synthetic biology could enhance their contributions to carbon sequestration as well as nutrient cycling, soil health, pollutant degradation, and ecosystem resilience.

But for HHMI investigator Harmit Malik and his team at the Fred Hutchinson Cancer Center, it's the genomes—not the people—that are in conflict. The lab studies rapid evolution—the genetic changes that happen in a species over a few generations rather than thousands of years. These fast changes are often fueled by genetic conflicts—competitions between different entities trying to maximize their success at the expense of another.
